story.title: Shopify opens checkout to browser-based AI agents

facts.text: Shopify previously supported WebMCP for its storefronts and carts, allowing browser-based AI agents to comb through a Shopify retailer’s inventory, search for products, and add them to a cart.

The addition of WebMCP support for checkout, including Shop Pay, means these agents can now read the checkout screen, update it, and submit the transaction with the buyer’s authorization, without relying on screenshots or scraping web pages, the company said.

While some retailers, like Amazon (and Adidas , apparently!), are blocking AI agents from making purchases on users’ behalf on their respective platforms, e-commerce platform Shopify has moved in the other direction.
Shopify already offers a hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which allows agents to work server-to-server.

“If your agent is operating in the buyer’s browser, use WebMCP tools provided on storefront and checkout to efficiently complete order placement, instead of navigating HTML built for humans,” Greenberg wrote on X. “These WebMCP tools provide structured and efficient APIs, purposely designed — via UCP — to ensure accurate commerce facts, required disclosures, and handoff requirements.”
Top AI agents like Muse and Instinct already have direct partnerships with Shopify for agentic commerce.
The Instinct partnership was announced today.
The feature is rolling out to all eligible Shopify merchants, said Gil Greenberg , a staff product manager who works on agentic commerce at Shopify, in a post on X .
Shopify previously supported WebMCP for its storefronts and carts, allowing browser-based AI agents to comb through a Shopify retailer's inventory, search for products, and add them to a cart.

The addition of WebMCP support for checkout, including Shop Pay, means these agents can now read the checkout screen, update it, and submit the transaction with the buyer's authorization, without relying on screenshots or scraping web pages, the company said.

While some retailers, like Amazon (and Adidas , apparently!), are blocking AI agents from making purchases on users' behalf on their respective platforms, e-commerce platform Shopify has moved in the other direction.
Shopify already offers a hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which allows agents to work server-to-server.
Both leverage Shopify's Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which provides a common way to search for and discover products, build carts, and check out.
Top AI agents like Muse and Instinct already have direct partnerships with Shopify for agentic commerce.
The Instinct partnership was announced today.
The feature is rolling out to all eligible Shopify merchants, said Gil Greenberg , a staff product manager who works on agentic commerce at Shopify, in a post on X .

This update introduces three new tools — get_checkout, update_checkout, and complete_checkout — that allow agents to inspect a checkout, change things like the customer's address or delivery option, and then place an order after the buyer authorizes it.
Shopify just turned every storefront on its platform into an AI agent playground.

On August 5, the company activated native WebMCP support across all Liquid storefronts and the Hydrogen developer preview, letting browser-based AI agents handle everything from product searches to checkout, no merchant setup required.
Instead of the approach where bots try to simulate mouse clicks and parse HTML, WebMCP creates a standardized set of tools that agents can call directly.
The tools Shopify has exposed through WebMCP include functions like search_catalog, update_cart, and proceed_to_checkout.

By explicitly blocking AI agents from handling payment credentials and requiring buyer consent before order finalization, Shopify has drawn a clear line that regulators and consumers can both understand.
The e-commerce giant's WebMCP rollout lets AI agents search catalogs, manage carts, and finalize orders directly in a shopper's browser session.
This builds on infrastructure Shopify had already been developing around MCP and UCP protocols, extending its existing compliance and security frameworks to cover these new agent-driven interactions.
© Decentral Media and Crypto Briefing® 2026.
Both companies have thrown support behind the WebMCP standard, which makes sense given that they control the two largest Chromium-based browsers.
Shopify Opens Every Storefront to AI Agents With New WebMCP Tools

Shopify's August 5 changelog announced WebMCP support for Liquid and Hydrogen storefronts, and its developer documentation says Shopify provides WebMCP tools on every Liquid storefront and storefronts built with the Hydrogen developer preview.
That means an AI agent riding along in a shopper's browser can now call structured commands: search the catalog, add an item to the cart, check a shipping policy, start checkout.
Shopify says the tools are live, but agent support is currently limited to Chromium-based browsers.
Chrome's own inspector extension can test WebMCP tools with Gemini by default, but Google says that extension is separate from Gemini in Chrome.
The storefront just exposes its own tools, and whichever agent shows up in the browser calls them directly against the live store.
WebMCP operates inside the shopper's own browser session, registering your storefront's functions directly with the browser the way a page registers a click handler.
Shopify is one of the biggest commerce platforms to switch it on by default for standard storefronts.

OpenAI launched Instant Checkout on September 29, 2025, with Etsy sellers live in ChatGPT and more than a million Shopify merchants announced as coming soon, built on the Agentic Commerce Protocol it developed with Stripe.
